title: Why Krishna keeps working
hookLine: who is the service for? the Gita draws the circle wider than anyone asked
carry: lokasangraha: act so the world holds together
tomorrow: a plan so big it's dead by spring. what does the Gita say?
last: START WITH WHAT'S IN YOUR HANDS.

cards: Every plan has a line near the top: who is this for? A food drive is for the hungry. A tutoring hour is for one kid.
Krishna answers that line for the path of action, and his answer is wider than anyone asked. Act, he tells Arjuna, with your eye on holding the world together.

teach.b: The Sanskrit is lokasangraha: loka, the world and the people in it; sangraha, a holding together. In chapter three of the Gita, Krishna gives the reason, and then he points at himself.
Whatever a great person does, others do too; the world follows the standard that person sets.
And, Krishna says, there's nothing in all the worlds I need to do, nothing I lack, and still I keep working. If I stopped, people everywhere would follow my path, and the worlds would fall apart.
God himself keeps working, for the sake of everyone watching. That's the teaching: in karma yoga, service reaches the one person helped, and also everyone who sees how it's done.
Now the week, one more pass. Kundalini climbs, lotus by lotus, to the crown, where Shakti and Shiva are one. Seed sounds on the petals: in a mantra, the sound itself is sacred.
A moon, a sun, and Ekalavya before his clay teacher: some practices are handed on, guru to student.
A rain cloud at the navel: in dhyana, you hold the form as it's given. The way home, down the same road, because the everyday world is Shakti too.
And Arjuna's dropped bow: no one can stop acting, so do your work and let go of the fruits.

how: Some Hindus think of service as including the example it sets for children, students and coworkers, reading the Gita's lokasangraha as care for the world that watches and follows.

o: action, done with the whole world in view
a ledger of favors that others owe you
fate that decides what happens to you

games.q: the week, and a wider circle — tap the pairs.
p: Krishna works, though he needs nothing
a rain cloud, held as given

games.q: you captain a team and quietly do the dull cleanup after every practice. a teammate says nobody notices, so why bother? what fits Gita 3.21?
o: others follow the standard set; doing it well is already teaching the team.
if nobody notices, it isn't really service, so stop.
make sure everyone sees you do it, or it doesn't count.
games.why: whatever a great person does, others do too. the standard set reaches the people watching, whether or not anyone says so.

practice: On a scrap of paper, draw three rings, one inside the next. In the center write one person you serve, in the middle ring the people who see you do it, and leave the outer ring open for the world.
Rest your eyes on all three together for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Karma: action, and in the Gita, action done with an eye on lokasangraha, the holding together of the world.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the holding together of the world; Krishna's word for what action keeps in view.

carryVoice: Last line of the week: lokasangraha, act so the world holds together. Even Krishna keeps working. Seven days, and a wider circle.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 3.20 (act with an eye to lokasangraha, the holding together of the world)
Bhagavad Gita 3.21 (whatever a great person does, others do; the world follows the standard set)
Bhagavad Gita 3.22–24 (Krishna: nothing in the three worlds I must do or lack, yet I keep acting; if I stopped, people would follow my path and the worlds would perish)
Bhagavad Gita 3.25 (as the unwise act attached, the wise should act unattached, wishing for lokasangraha)
